doc.title: John Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Family separation and copyist Herbie Jones
summary: Leaving his wife was hard; encouragement came from Mrs. Reed and from copyist Herbie Jones.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: Did it get hard with your family situation?

Oh yes. It was hard. I’ll never forget the look on my wife’s face the night that I went on the road. I wish I could take that face and just transform it into something else, but it was a look — a true sense of separation. But we received a lot of encouragement from people that had been on the road for a while. The wives. The people like Mrs. Reed, she encouraged us quite a bit. And she kept in contact with my wife. And she said the sound is important. And a guy sat on the bus one day and he says, “hey John, don’t play this thing cheaply,” he says, “this is going to be very important one of these days.” He says, “I know how you feel but it’s important. People love this guy.” He was one of the copyists for the band. He went through his headaches trying to copy Duke’s music. Because he didn’t copy for each instrument, he copied for individuals. He’d have the
lines all crossed and he’d have to siphon through all these lines. And he understood, you know, the techniques. Herbie Jones was the copyist.
Yeah, that must have been a chore.

Sure, he wrote his lines for each person. And it all came out — it sounded distorted to them but to Duke, that’s what he wanted. And he always found a way to incorporate each new personality into the band.
